3 0.000 0.008 0.000
4 0.000 0.002 0.000

The sample ACF of the second differences matches the theoretical values, and is zero beyond lag 2. A fitted MA(2) reproduces the same ACF.

Question 4: Regression coefficients with a Kalman filter

The tutorial uses usconsumption from the (older) fpp package. The same quarterly growth rates for US personal consumption and disposable income are in uschange in fpp2 (with more recent data, 1970–2016), so I used those.

Click to toggle source code 
# Read in data:
data(uschange)
# View(uschange)

y_us = uschange[, "Consumption"]
z_us = uschange[, "Income"]

Figure 55 shows that consumption and income growth move together, but income growth is much more volatile, and the scatter plot shows a positive but noisy relationship.

Click to toggle source code 
# Ordinary least squares:
lm_us = lm(y_us ~ z_us)
summary(lm_us)$coefficients
             Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 0.5451038 0.05568668 9.788765 1.700914e-18
z_us        0.2806012 0.04744194 5.914624 1.577409e-08

The Kalman filter for regression

As a state-space model, \(\theta_t = (a_t, b_t)'\), \(G = I\), \(W = 0\) (the coefficients do not change), \(F_t = (1, z_t)\) and \(V = \sigma^2\). This is my kalman_filter() with \(F_t\) given as a function of \(t\):

Click to toggle source code 
n_us = length(y_us)
z_vec = as.numeric(z_us)

kf_reg = function(sigma2) {
  kalman_filter(as.numeric(y_us), FF = function(t) c(1, z_vec[t]), GG = diag(2),
                V = sigma2, W = matrix(0, 2, 2), m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1e7, 2))
}

kf_us_1 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 1)
kf_us_100 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 100)

# Filtered coefficients and diagonal of C_t (without time-0 row):
coef_path = kf_us_1$m[-1, ]
C_diag = t(sapply(kf_us_1$C[-1], diag))

kable(data.frame(
  Coefficient = c("a (intercept)", "b (slope)"),
  OLS = coef(lm_us),
  KF_sigma2_1 = kf_us_1$m[n_us + 1, ],
  KF_sigma2_100 = kf_us_100$m[n_us + 1, ]
), digits = 5, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Coefficient", "OLS", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 1$)", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 100$)"))
Coefficient OLS Kalman filter (\(\sigma^2 = 1\)) Kalman filter (\(\sigma^2 = 100\))
a (intercept) 0.5451 0.5451 0.5451
b (slope) 0.2806 0.2806 0.2806

The final filtered estimates \(m_T\) are identical to the OLS estimates (up to the effect of the very vague prior), whatever value of \(\sigma^2\) is used.

Why \(\sigma^2\) does not matter

With \(W = 0\) and a prior variance proportional to \(\sigma^2\) (\(C_0 = \sigma^2 C_0^*\)), every variance in the filter (\(R_t\), \(C_t\) and \(Q_t\)) is proportional to \(\sigma^2\). The Kalman gain \(K_t = R_tF_t'/Q_t\) is a ratio of these, so \(\sigma^2\) cancels and the filtered means \(m_t\) do not depend on it. Only the variances \(C_t\) do. Here \(C_0 = 10^7 I\) is fixed rather than scaled by \(\sigma^2\), but it is so vague that its effect on \(m_t\) is negligible for both \(\sigma^2 = 1\) and \(\sigma^2 = 100\).

Estimating \(\sigma^2\)

Run the filter with \(\sigma^2 = 1\). The standardised prediction errors \(e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}\) then have variance \(\sigma^2\). The first two have (almost) zero weight because the prior is vague and two coefficients have to be learned first, so

\[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t=3}^{T} \frac{e_t^2}{Q_t}. \]

Click to toggle source code 
sigma2_kf = sum(kf_us_1$e[-(1:2)]^2 / kf_us_1$Q[-(1:2)]) / (n_us - 2)
c(kalman_filter = sigma2_kf, lm = summary(lm_us)$sigma^2)
kalman_filter            lm 
    0.3631358     0.3631358

These are the same: the sum of squared standardised one-step-ahead errors (the recursive residuals) equals the OLS residual sum of squares.

Recursive coefficient estimates

\(m_t\) is (up to the vague prior) the OLS estimate using only the data up to quarter \(t\) (Figure 56). If the relationship were constant, these estimates should settle down and then only fluctuate within their intervals. Systematic drift (for example a slope that keeps decreasing) suggests that the coefficients change over time.

Here the estimates do not settle down smoothly. After the noisy start, the slope stays around 0.4 to 0.5 until the early 1980s and then drifts down to the full-sample value of about 0.28, with sudden jumps around 1980, 2001 and 2013. Even after 100 or more quarters a single quarter can move the recursive slope noticeably, which suggests that a few quarters with unusually large income changes are influential, or that the relationship has changed over time.

Recursive estimates are a weak test, though, because every new estimate still uses all the earlier data. A more direct approach is to let the coefficients follow random walks (\(W > 0\)) and compare the likelihoods.

Click to toggle source code 
# Static (W = 0) vs time-varying (W estimated) coefficients:
build_static = function(p) dlmModReg(z_us, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = c(0, 0))
build_tvp = function(p) dlmModReg(z_us, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = exp(p[2:3]))

fit_static = dlmMLE(y_us, parm = log(var(y_us)), build = build_static, method = "BFGS")
fit_tvp = dlmMLE(y_us, parm = c(log(var(y_us)), -5, -5), build = build_tvp)

kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Static coefficients", "Time-varying coefficients"),
  Parameters = c(1, 3),
  neg_loglik = c(fit_static$value, fit_tvp$value),
  AIC = c(2 * fit_static$value + 2 * 1, 2 * fit_tvp$value + 2 * 3)
), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Model", "Parameters", "$-\\log L$", "AIC"))
Model Parameters \(-\log L\) AIC
Static coefficients 1 20.07 42.15
Time-varying coefficients 3 9.56 25.13
Click to toggle source code 
signif(exp(fit_tvp$par), 3)  # V, W_a, W_b
[1] 0.19500 0.03280 0.00647

The time-varying coefficient model has a much lower AIC (25.1 vs 42.1), and neither coefficient variance is close to zero (\(\hat{W}_a = 0.033\), \(\hat{W}_b =0.0065\)). The observation variance drops from about 0.36 to 0.2. So the data favour coefficients that change over time. (Because \(W = 0\) lies on the boundary of the parameter space, the usual \(\chi^2\) reference distribution for a likelihood ratio test does not apply, but the AIC difference is large enough for this not to matter.) The smoothed coefficients (Figure 57) show how the relationship evolved. The slope is highest (about 0.5 to 0.6) in the 1970s and falls to around 0.1 after 2000, so consumption growth has become less sensitive to income growth. The intercept moves a lot and drops sharply in the 2008–2009 recession, so the random-walk intercept also picks up slow movements in consumption growth that income does not explain:

Hidden Markov Models

This section works through Questions 1 to 7 of the HMM tutorial. It uses the HMM toolkit (scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm and the stationary distribution) that I wrote from first principles for Project 4, where the toolkit is explained in detail. Question 8, Poisson HMMs for the earthquake counts, is in Project 4, because it is where I checked the toolkit against depmixS4 before applying it to JSE returns.

Click to toggle source code 
library(tidyverse)

# Same seed and colours as in Project 4:
set.seed(2026)
col_main   = "purple"
col_accent = "deeppink"
state_cols = c("1" = "steelblue", "2" = "purple", "3" = "deeppink", "4" = "black")
HMM toolkit (scripts/hmm-toolkit.R) 
# =============================================================================
# HMM toolkit, written from first principles (Time Series Analysis portfolio)
#
# Used by projects/project-04-analysis.qmd and section-2/section-2.qmd.
# Every function works with the matrix of state-dependent densities
# dens[t, i] = p_i(x_t), so the same code handles Poisson, Gaussian and
# categorical observations.
# =============================================================================

# Log-likelihood only (fast version, used inside optim()):
hmm_loglik = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  v = delta * dens[1, ]
  ll = log(sum(v))
  phi = v / sum(v)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      v = as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
      u = sum(v)
      ll = ll + log(u)
      phi = v / u
    }
  }
  ll
}

# Scaled forward algorithm: log-likelihood, log u_t, filtered probabilities and log alpha:
hmm_forward = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  phi_mat = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  lu = numeric(T_len)
  for (t in 1:T_len) {
    v = if (t == 1) delta * dens[1, ] else as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
    u = sum(v)
    lu[t] = log(u)                # log p(x_t | x_{1:t-1})
    phi = v / u                   # P(C_t = i | x_{1:t})
    phi_mat[t, ] = phi
  }
  list(loglik = sum(lu), lu = lu, phi = phi_mat,
       lalpha = cumsum(lu) + log(phi_mat))   # log alpha_t(i)
}

# Scaled backward algorithm: log beta (Zucchini et al., 2016):
hmm_backward = function(dens, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lbeta = matrix(0, T_len, m)     # log beta_T = 0
  phi = rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale = log(m)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      v = as.numeric(Gamma %*% (dens[t + 1, ] * phi))
      lbeta[t, ] = log(v) + lscale
      phi = v / sum(v)
      lscale = lscale + log(sum(v))
    }
  }
  lbeta
}

# Local decoding: P(C_t = i | x_{1:T}) = alpha_t(i) beta_t(i) / L_T:
hmm_local = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens, delta, Gamma)
  lbeta = hmm_backward(dens, Gamma)
  exp(fwd$lalpha + lbeta - fwd$loglik)
}

# Global decoding with the Viterbi algorithm (log scale):
hmm_viterbi = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lG = log(Gamma)
  ld = log(dens)
  xi = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  xi[1, ] = log(delta) + ld[1, ]
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      for (j in 1:m) {
        xi[t, j] = max(xi[t - 1, ] + lG[, j]) + ld[t, j]
      }
    }
  }
  # Back-tracing:
  states = numeric(T_len)
  states[T_len] = which.max(xi[T_len, ])
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      states[t] = which.max(xi[t, ] + lG[, states[t + 1]])
    }
  }
  list(states = states, xi = xi)
}

# Stationary distribution: solve delta (I - Gamma + U) = 1:
stat_dist = function(Gamma) {
  m = nrow(Gamma)
  solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
}

# Working (unconstrained) parameters -> transition probability matrix:
gamma_w2n = function(w, m) {
  G = diag(m)
  G[!G] = exp(w)                  # off-diagonal elements, relative to the diagonal
  G / rowSums(G)
}

# h-step transition matrix Gamma^h:
mat_pow = function(M, h) {
  R = diag(nrow(M))
  for (i in seq_len(h)) R = R %*% M
  R
}

Figure 58 shows the three state distributions: state 1 is centred at \((-10, 0)\) with positive correlation, state 2 at \((10, 0)\) with negative correlation and state 3 at \((0, 10)\) with a much larger variance in \(x_1\) than in \(x_2\). Because the diagonal of \(\Gamma\) is 0.8, the process stays in a state for five steps on average (\(1/(1-0.8)\)), so consecutive points tend to come from the same cluster, and the path jumps between clusters only occasionally.

Given only the observations, we would need:

  • the transition probabilities: \(3 \times 2 = 6\),
  • the state means: \(3 \times 2 = 6\),
  • the covariance matrices: \(3 \times 3 = 9\),
  • the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\): 2 more.

That is 21 parameters (23 with \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\)), estimated from 20 bivariate observations (40 numbers). With so few observations the estimates would be very unreliable, and some states might not be visited often enough to estimate their covariance matrices at all.

9 z -13.256 -12.198 -12.604 B 0.116 0.485 0.399 B
10 y -15.559 -13.402 -14.319 B 0.111 0.536 0.354 B

The Viterbi algorithm fills in \(\xi_{ti}\), the log-probability of the most likely path that ends in state \(i\) at time \(t\) (together with the observations up to \(t\)):

\[ \xi_{1i} = \log\delta_i + \log p_i(x_1), \qquad \xi_{tj} = \max_i\left(\xi_{t-1,i} + \log\gamma_{ij}\right) + \log p_j(x_t). \]

The most likely final state is the one with the largest \(\xi_{Ti}\), and the path is traced back with \(S_t = \text{argmax}_i(\xi_{ti} + \log\gamma_{i,S_{t+1}})\). Working on the log scale turns the products into sums and avoids underflow.

The most likely state sequence is AAAAAAABBB, which agrees with the true sequence at 9 of the 10 time points. The first seven observations are all “x”, which state A emits with probability 0.6 (compared with 0.1 and 0.3 for B and C). A is the least persistent state (\(\gamma_{AA} = 0.5\)), but the emission probabilities outweigh this, so the algorithm stays in A. At time 8 the path switches to B. “z” is equally likely in B and C (0.4), and B and C are equally persistent (\(\gamma_{BB} = \gamma_{CC} = 0.6\)), but A moves to B more often than to C (0.3 vs 0.2) and the final “y” is more likely in B (0.5 vs 0.3).

The only mistake is at time 2, where the true state is C. A single “x” from C between “x”s from A is impossible to detect: it would need two unlikely transitions (A to C and C to A), and “x” is more likely in A anyway. This illustrates the main limitation of decoding: when the state distributions overlap, short visits to a state cannot be recovered. The local decoding probabilities in the table give the same sequence here, but they also show the uncertainty: \(P(A \mid \mathbf{x})\) is only about 0.75 for the first observations, and at time 8 the probabilities for B and C are close.

Question 3: Probability of three observations from a Poisson HMM

The two-state Poisson HMM has \(\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.1 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (1, 3)\). Since the HMM is stationary, \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is the stationary distribution, which solves \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\Gamma = \boldsymbol{\delta}\): \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = (4/13, 9/13)\).

a) Summing over all \(2^3 = 8\) state sequences:

\[ P(X_1 = 0, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 1) = \sum_{c_1, c_2, c_3} \delta_{c_1}\gamma_{c_1c_2}\gamma_{c_2c_3} \, p_{c_1}(0)\,p_{c_2}(2)\,p_{c_3}(1). \]

lambda_q3 = c(1, 3)
delta_q3 = stat_dist(Gamma_q3)
x_q3 = c(0, 2, 1)

paths = expand.grid(C1 = 1:2, C2 = 1:2, C3 = 1:2) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(`P(states)` = delta_q3[C1] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C1, C2)] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C2, C3)],
         `P(x | states)` = dpois(x_q3[1], lambda_q3[C1]) * dpois(x_q3[2], lambda_q3[C2]) *
                           dpois(x_q3[3], lambda_q3[C3]),
         Product = `P(states)` * `P(x | states)`) |>
  arrange(C1, C2, C3)

kable(paths, digits = 6)

c(delta = delta_q3,
  sum_over_paths = sum(paths$Product),
  matrix_formula = as.numeric(delta_q3 %*% P_q3(0) %*% Gamma_q3 %*% P_q3(2) %*%

Both methods give \(P(X_1 = 0, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 1) = 0.007292\). The matrix formula does the same sum, but by summing over the state at each time point as it goes, instead of listing every sequence. With \(m\) states and \(T\) observations, listing the sequences takes \(m^T\) terms (each a product of about \(2T\) factors), while the matrix product (the forward algorithm) takes about \(Tm^2\) operations. Table 17 also shows that the sequence (1, 2, 1) contributes most: a 0 is most likely from state 1 (\(\lambda = 1\)), a 2 is more likely from state 2 (\(\lambda = 3\)), and a 1 is again more likely from state 1. The transitions \(1 \to 2\) (0.9) and \(2 \to 1\) (0.4) are also reasonably likely.

Question 4: The independent mixture as a special case

If the Markov chain degenerates to a sequence of independent random variables, then \(P(C_t = j \mid C_{t-1} = i) = P(C_t = j) = \delta_j\) for every \(i\). So every row of \(\Gamma\) equals \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\), i.e. \(\Gamma = \mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is also the initial distribution. Then for any \(x\),

\[ \mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\Gamma = \mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta}, \]

and therefore every factor can be split off:

\[ \begin{aligned} L_T &= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\Gamma\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\ &= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_2)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\cdots\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\ &= \prod_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i\,p_i(x_t;\theta_i), \end{aligned} \]

because each \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \sum_i \delta_i p_i(x_t)\) is a scalar. This is the likelihood of an independent mixture model with mixing weights \(\delta_1, \dots, \delta_m\), as required.

      digits = 3)
Run Segments Total symbols Mean run length Estimated stay probability
A (before the B’s) 21 75 3.571 0.72
B 21 42 2.000 0.50

The string has a very regular structure. It always cycles through

\[ \underbrace{A\cdots A}_{\text{run of A's}}\ \underbrace{B\cdots B}_{\text{run of B's}}\ A\ C, \]

followed by the next run of A’s (the last segment, a single “A”, is the start of a new cycle). C is always preceded and followed by an A, and a run of B’s is always followed by exactly one A and then a C. So an “A” behaves differently depending on where it is: after a C, an A can be followed by more A’s or by a B, but after a B, an A is always followed by a C. One state for A is therefore not enough, and I propose a four-state HMM (Table 18):

Table 18: Proposed HMM for the first string.
State Emits Transitions
1: “A-run” A (probability 1) stay in 1 with probability \(p_A\), move to 2 with \(1-p_A\)
2: “B-run” B (probability 1) stay in 2 with probability \(p_B\), move to 3 with \(1-p_B\)
3: “single A” A (probability 1) move to 4 with probability 1
4: “C” C (probability 1) move to 1 with probability 1

\[ \Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} p_A & 1-p_A & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & p_B & 1-p_B & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \ (\text{columns: A, B, C}), \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0, 0). \]

The string starts with a run of A’s, so the initial state is 1. The time spent in a state with stay probability \(p\) is geometric with mean \(1/(1-p)\), so \(p\) can be estimated from the run lengths: \(\hat{p} = (\text{total symbols} - \text{number of runs})/\text{total symbols}\). This gives \(\hat{p}_A = 0.72\) and \(\hat{p}_B = 0.5\) (mean runs of 3.6 A’s and 2 B’s). In this model the emissions are deterministic, so the “hidden” part is only that two states emit A. It is still an HMM, because A from state 1 and A from state 3 cannot be told apart without the context.

The 60 symbols split into 20 triplets, and each position of a triplet uses its own pair of symbols: the first symbol is always B or C, the second always A or E, and the third always D or F. This is a three-state HMM with a deterministic cycle:

\[ \Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0), \]

The cross-table of the first and second symbols shows that B and C are each followed by A and E about equally often, so it is reasonable to treat the emissions as independent given the state, which is what an HMM assumes. Question 6: The occasionally dishonest casino

This is the classic example from Durbin et al. (1998). A fair die (state 1) and a loaded die that rolls a six half of the time (state 2) are switched according to \(\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.05 \\ 0.10 & 0.90 \end{pmatrix}\).

The chain spends about a third of the time with the loaded die (\(\delta_2 = 1/3\)), and in the simulation sixes are much more frequent when the loaded die is used. The Viterbi path recovers the die correctly for 82% of the rolls (Figure 59). Decoding works because the loaded die is used for runs of about 10 rolls (\(1/(1-0.9)\)), so a cluster of sixes is good evidence of a switch. Short visits to the loaded die are usually missed, and the switches are detected a few rolls late, because a single six is also quite likely from the fair die.

Question 7: A two-state Bernoulli HMM

With \(P(X_t = x \mid C_t = 1) = 0.5\) for \(x = 0, 1\) and \(P(X_t = 1 \mid C_t = 2) = 1\),

\[ \mathbf{P}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{P}(1) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Click to toggle source code 
Gamma_q7 = matrix(c(0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
delta_q7 = c(1, 2) / 3
p1_q7 = c(0.5, 1)                         # P(X = 1 | C = i)

P_q7 = function(x) diag(if (x == 1) p1_q7 else 1 - p1_q7)

# Likelihood with the matrix product:
bern_hmm_lik = function(x, delta, Gamma) {
  L = delta %*% P_q7(x[1])
  for (t in seq_along(x)[-1]) L = L %*% Gamma %*% P_q7(x[t])
  as.numeric(L %*% rep(1, length(delta)))
}

c(check_stationary = stat_dist(Gamma_q7),
  P_X_equals_0 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(0) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  P_X_equals_1 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(1) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  L_111 = bern_hmm_lik(c(1, 1, 1), delta_q7, Gamma_q7),
  `29/48` = 29 / 48,
  L_111_forward = exp(hmm_loglik(t(sapply(c(1, 1, 1), function(x) diag(P_q7(x)))), delta_q7, Gamma_q7)))
check_stationary1 check_stationary2      P_X_equals_0      P_X_equals_1 
        0.3333333         0.6666667         0.1666667         0.8333333 
            L_111             29/48     L_111_forward 
        0.6041667         0.6041667         0.6041667

The stationary distribution is \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = \frac{1}{3}(1, 2)\), so marginally \(P(X_t = 0) = \frac{1}{3}(0.5) = 1/6\) and \(P(X_t = 1) = 5/6\). The likelihood of three 1’s is \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\mathbf{1}' = 29/48 \approx 0.604\), which both my matrix-product function and my forward algorithm reproduce. This is larger than \((5/6)^3 \approx 0.579\), the value if the observations were independent, because a 1 makes state 2 more likely, and state 2 is persistent and always emits 1.

References

  • Durbin, R., Eddy, S. R., Krogh, A., & Mitchison, G. (1998). Biological sequence analysis: Probabilistic models of proteins and nucleic acids. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zucchini, W., MacDonald, I. L., & Langrock, R. (2016). Hidden Markov models for time series: An introduction using R (2nd ed.). CRC Press.

Project 1

Forecasting South African daily electricity demand with exponential smoothing

Section and topic: Section 2 - Exponential smoothing (Holt-Winters and ETS state-space models).

Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. Additive Holt-Winters (ETS(A,N,A)) coded from first principles, including its prediction intervals.

Aim: To forecast daily South African electricity demand 1 to 14 days ahead with exponential smoothing. To determine which exponential smoothing model forecasts best compared to the naive and seasonal naive benchmarks, whether its prediction intervals are reliable, and whether removing the annual cycle improves the forecasts.

Data used:

  • Hourly RSA contracted demand (MW), 1 April 2019 to 13 September 2023. Source: Eskom (2024), Eskom Data Portal, https://www.eskom.co.za/dataportal/. The data are aggregated system totals with no personal information.

The hourly data were averaged to daily mean demand. The models use 1 March 2021 to 13 September 2023, which leaves out the 2020 lockdown period. The training set ends on 19 July 2023 (871 days). Its last 8 weeks are a validation window for modelling choices. The last 8 weeks of the data (20 July 2023 to 13 September 2023) are the test set. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis.

Methods used: A Bai-Perron structural break test (with a sensitivity check on the minimum segment length) to choose the start date. Time plots, day-of-week boxplots, the ACF and an MSTL decomposition into weekly and annual components. SES, additive Holt-Winters with and without a damped trend and multiplicative Holt-Winters were fitted as ETS state-space models with forecast::ets() and compared by AICc. ETS(A,N,A) was also implemented from first principles: the error-correction filter, estimation by minimising the SSE with optim(), and the analytic forecast variance. Residual diagnostics included the Ljung-Box test and an analysis of the largest residuals against public holidays. The forecasts were evaluated against the naive and seasonal naive benchmarks with a rolling forecast origin (horizons 1 to 14 days, RMSE, MAE, MAPE and the Diebold-Mariano test). The coverage of the model-based prediction intervals was compared with empirical intervals built from in-sample multi-step errors. As an extension, a deterministic annual cycle (Fourier terms) was removed before smoothing, and this choice was made on the validation window rather than the test set.

Key findings:

  • The end of the lockdown disruption falls between 14 September 2020 and 22 March 2021 depending on the minimum segment length, so the modelling period starts on 1 March 2021, the move to alert level 1.
  • Daily demand has a strong and stable weekly pattern (Sunday demand is about 1,300 MW below the level and Tuesday to Thursday about 500 to 600 MW above it), a winter peak and no long-term trend. ETS(A,N,A) had the lowest AICc, which agrees with automatic selection (ETS(A,N,A)).
  • The estimates are \(\hat{\alpha} \approx\) 0.92 and \(\hat{\gamma} \approx 0\): the weekly pattern is fixed while the level moves almost like a random walk. My filter reproduces the ets() residuals exactly (maximum difference 3.6^{-12} MW). Estimated independently, my optimiser reached the boundary (\(\hat{\alpha} \approx\) 1) with a marginally lower SSE, which shows how flat the likelihood is in \(\alpha\).
  • Out of sample, ETS(A,N,A) had an RMSE of 674 MW (MAPE 2.1%), compared with 786 MW for the seasonal naive and 1,185 MW for the naive benchmark. My own code gave 675 MW. One day ahead it roughly halved the seasonal naive error (326 vs 658 MW, Diebold-Mariano p-value <0.001), but at 7 and 14 days ahead the two were equally accurate (p-values 0.8 and 0.86).
  • 10 of the 10 largest residuals fall on a public holiday or the day after one. The residuals are autocorrelated and heavy-tailed (excess kurtosis 3.7).
  • The model-based prediction intervals were too wide (the 80% intervals covered 94% of the test values), because \(\hat{\alpha} \approx 1\) implies that uncertainty grows like a random walk and holidays inflate \(\hat{\sigma}\). Empirical intervals gave 83% coverage at the 80% level.
  • Removing the annual cycle gave opposite results in the two periods: worse on the validation window (RMSE 713 to 788 MW) and better on the test set (674 to 595 MW). The 2023 winter peak was much lower than in earlier years (mean June demand 27,200 MW in 2022 and 26,500 MW in 2023), so a fixed annual cycle is not reliable. It was left out of the final model.
  • The final forecast carries the high demand at the end of the series (27,588 MW, against 26,447 MW on the same day a week earlier) into every forecast for the next two weeks. This is the main practical weakness of a level with \(\hat{\alpha}\) close to 1.

What I would do differently next time:

  • Make modelling choices on a validation window from the start. I first judged the annual adjustment on the test set, where it looked like a clear improvement. On the validation window it made the forecasts worse.
  • Model public holidays explicitly, for example with holiday indicators in a regression with ETS errors, since they cause the largest errors and inflate the prediction intervals.
  • Use a method designed for multiple seasonal patterns (TBATS or double seasonal Holt-Winters), with temperature and load shedding as predictors, instead of a fixed annual adjustment.
  • Evaluate over several rolling windows covering a full year, including the Christmas period, and model unconstrained demand (adding back the load that was shed) rather than the demand that was actually supplied.

Link to the detailed analysis: Detailed analysis and code

Project 2

Predicting drought in the Western Cape

Section and topic: Section 1 - Linear models for the conditional mean (seasonal ARIMA and dynamic regression).

Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. Includes a prewhitened cross-correlation analysis and a composition adjustment for incomplete buoy data.

Aim: To determine whether Theewaterskloof Dam capacity and eastern Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) can be forecast with seasonal ARIMA models, and whether lagged SST, as a leading indicator of El Niño, improves dam capacity forecasts.

Data used:

  • Daily Theewaterskloof Dam levels (% of capacity), January 2000 to January 2026. Source: City of Cape Town Open Data Portal, Dam levels from 2000, https://odp-cctegis.opendata.arcgis.com/.
  • Daily SST (°C) from the seven TAO/TRITON buoys along 95°W, January 2000 to April 2026 (models fitted to January 2000 to October 2021 because of long gaps in the record). Source: NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory, https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/tao/drupal/disdel/.

Both series were aggregated to monthly means. Neither dataset contains personal information. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis and the code and data appendix.

Methods used: STL decomposition, ACF/PACF and unit root tests to choose the differencing and candidate orders. Seven seasonal ARIMA candidates selected by rolling-origin cross-validation (with AICc as a check) on the training data only, then evaluated once on a held-out test set against Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive, Drift and ETS(A,N,A). A prewhitened cross-correlation to choose the SST lag, a time series linear model, and a dynamic regression (SARIMAX). Accuracy measured with RMSE, MAE, MAPE and CRPS; residuals checked with Ljung-Box tests.

Key findings:

  • The selected dam capacity model is ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] (test CRPS = 4.828, ranked 1 of 6 models, against 9.164 for Seasonal naive). Most of the predictability comes from the dam’s own persistence and seasonality.
  • The selected SST model is ARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] (test CRPS = 0.585, ranked 2 of 6). It performed very similarly to the Seasonal naive model on the short SST test set, with a slightly higher CRPS but lower RMSE, MAE and MAPE.
  • The two-year dam capacity forecast keeps the seasonal cycle (monthly means between 43.1% and 77.6%), but the 95% prediction interval widens to about 66 percentage points by the end of the horizon and exceeds 100% capacity. The dam model’s residuals are not fully white noise (Ljung-Box \(p\) = 0.001), so these intervals are probably too narrow.
  • The raw cross-correlation between dam levels and SST is dominated by their five-to-six-month seasonal offset, not by El Niño. After prewhitening, the strongest lead is at 10 months (CCF = -0.091), with 0 of 12 lead lags outside the 95% bounds.
  • A time series linear model finds a significant negative relationship between lagged SST and dam levels (\(\hat\beta\) = -2.779, \(p\) = 0.012), as hypothesised, but its residuals are strongly autocorrelated. With ARIMA errors, the SST coefficient is -0.341 (\(p\) = 0.663), and the dynamic regression’s forecasts (CRPS = 18.852) are no better than the univariate model’s (18.700).
  • There is no statistically significant evidence that SST at 95°W is a useful monthly leading indicator of Theewaterskloof Dam levels.
  • Forecast rankings depend on the test window: the Naive model beat the ARIMA model during the 2019–2021 post-drought recovery. This is why selection used cross-validation rather than a single test set.
  • Gaps in the buoy record from November 2021 meant that no model could forecast into the 2026/2027 El Niño period.
  • Model logit-transformed capacity so that prediction intervals stay within 0-100%.

What I would do differently next time:

  • Use catchment rainfall and water-use data as predictors, since they drive dam inflow and outflow directly.
  • Use a gap-free ENSO index, such as the Oceanic Niño Index, instead of a single buoy line, so that forecasts could reach 2027.
  • Fit a regime-switching model that allows the SST–dam relationship to differ between El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases.
  • Model logit-transformed capacity so that prediction intervals stay within 0–100%.

Project 3

Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns

Section and topic: Section 1 - Conditional variance models (ARCH and GARCH).

Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. The GARCH(1,1) likelihood is coded from first principles.

Aim: To model and forecast the volatility of daily JSE All Share Index (ALSI) returns, and to determine which model, ARCH, GARCH or GJR-GARCH, gives the best out-of-sample volatility forecasts compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks.

Data used:

  • Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203, dividends reinvested), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. Source: Gebbie, T. (2020), Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017, University of Cape Town, https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1.

Daily log returns (%) were modelled. July 1995 to December 2012 is used as the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 as the test set. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis.

Methods used: The mean equation is selected by comparing candidate ARIMA models using BIC. The residuals of this model are tested for ARCH effects using the Ljung-Box test on the squared residuals and Engle’s ARCH LM test. The order of a pure ARCH model is chosen using BIC and compared to a GARCH(\(1,1\)) model with the same mean and normal innovations. The candidate models, ARCH(\(q\)), GARCH(\(1,1\)) with normal and Student-\(t\) innovations and GJR-GARCH(\(1,1\)) with Student-\(t\) innovations, are estimated by maximum likelihood. The GARCH(\(1,1\)) likelihood is coded from first principles and maximised using optim. The fitted models are assessed using diagnostics on the standardised residuals. The rolling one-day ahead volatility forecasts are compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks using MSE and QLIKE, Diebold–Mariano tests of equal predictive accuracy and Value-at-Risk backtests. The optimal model is used to forecast volatility over the following 63 trading days.

Key findings:

  • The returns are only weakly autocorrelated, so an AR(1) mean model is sufficient. However, there is strong evidence of ARCH effects (\(p\) < 0.001). Thus, volatility is predictable even though returns are not.
  • A pure ARCH model requires 11 lags and still has a higher BIC than a GARCH(1,1) model. Volatility shocks in the ARCH model have a half-life < 5 trading days as opposed to the GARCH models with half-lives ranging from 55 to 98 trading days.
  • GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-\(t\) errors is the best model both in sample (BIC = 2.983) and out of sample (QLIKE = 0.805), outperforming EWMA (QLIKE = 0.849) and the constant-variance model (QLIKE = 1.063). Negative shocks increase the following day’s variance approximately 2.8 times more than positive shocks of the same size. Volatility is highly persistent (persistence = 0.987) and the errors have heavier tails than the normal distribution (\(\hat{\nu} = 9.9\)).
  • Diebold–Mariano tests show that at the 5% level, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) has a significantly lower QLIKE loss than Constant, EWMA, ARCH, GARCH-N and GARCH-\(t\).
  • Value-at-Risk backtests show that at the 1% level, Constant, GARCH-\(t\) and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) pass both tests, while EWMA, ARCH and GARCH-N are rejected by at least one test.
  • My implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood, from first principles, reproduced the rugarch estimates to 3 decimal places.
  • At the end of the sample, volatility (13.0% p.a.) is below its long-run level (19.0% p.a.). Thus, the forecast rises slowly towards the long-run level and reaches 16.8% p.a. after 63 trading days.

What I would do differently next time:

  • The returns are negatively skewed, which a symmetric Student-\(t\) distribution cannot capture. I would compare the models with skewed Student-\(t\) innovations.
  • I would extend the dataset beyond February 2017. This would allow for current volatility forecasts and would test the stability of the estimated parameters.

Link to the detailed analysis: Detailed analysis and code

Project 4

Hidden Markov models: from first principles to market regimes on the JSE

Section and topic: Section 2 - Hidden Markov models (likelihood, forward and backward probabilities, local and global decoding, forecasting).

Type of project: Implementation (all core HMM algorithms coded from first principles and checked against depmixS4), extended to model comparison on real-world data, with an interactive Shiny app.

Aim: To implement the HMM algorithms from first principles, validate them on the tutorial’s earthquake data. Use the HMM algorithms to determine whether daily JSE All Share Index returns can be described by a small number of market regimes, when these regimes occurred, and whether a Gaussian HMM forecasts the distribution of returns as well as the GJR-GARCH model from Project 3.

Data used:

  • Annual counts of major earthquakes (magnitude 7 and above), 1900–2006. Source: Zucchini, MacDonald and Langrock (2016), as in the course notes and tutorial.
  • Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. Source: Gebbie, T. (2020), Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017, University of Cape Town, https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1.

Daily log returns (%) were modelled, with July 1995 to December 2012 as the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 as the test set (as in Project 3). Download instructions are in the detailed analysis and the code and data appendix.

Methods used: I implemented the main HMM algorithms from first principles: the scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, the stationary distribution and forecast distributions. Parameters were estimated by numerically maximising the likelihood with nlm() and optim() on unconstrained working parameters. The implementation was validated against depmixS4 using Poisson HMMs for the earthquake counts; the remaining tutorial questions are in the Hidden Markov Models section of Section 2.

For the JSE returns, Gaussian HMMs with one to four states were fitted from several sets of starting values and compared using AIC and BIC. The selected model was assessed with normal pseudo-residuals, decoded with the Viterbi algorithm and local decoding, and given approximate standard errors using the Hessian and the delta method. It was then compared with GJR-GARCH(1,1)-\(t\) using filtered volatility and one-step-ahead log scores on the test set, with a Newey-West test of equal predictive ability. A Shiny app presents the fitted regimes interactively.

Key findings:

  • My likelihood code reproduced the depmixS4 log-likelihoods for the earthquake data exactly (−341.88 and −328.53), but only once the initial distribution was estimated freely, as depmixS4 does. A three-state Poisson HMM (about 13, 20 and 30 earthquakes per year) is selected by both AIC and BIC.
  • For JSE returns, BIC selects four regimes, although three regimes already remove the heavy tails and the volatility clustering from the pseudo-residuals. The regimes range from a calm market (annualised volatility of about 8%) to a crisis regime (about 45%) with a negative mean return, which lasts about 20 trading days on average and is entered gradually through the intermediate regimes.
  • The crisis regime picks out the 1998 emerging market crisis andmthe 2008–2009 global financial crisis. The HMM’s real-time (filtered) volatility is strongly correlated with the GJR-GARCH volatility.
  • With its default starting values, depmixS4 stopped at a one-state solution for the JSE data, so I refitted it with starting values for a calm and a turbulent state. This showed how easily an optimiser can stop at the wrong point.
  • Out of sample, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) forecasts the next day’s return distribution significantly better than every HMM (log score −1.317 compared with −1.326 for the best HMM). HMMs are useful for describing market regimes, while GARCH remains better for forecasting risk.

What I would do differently next time:

  • Use a parametric bootstrap instead of the delta method for confidence intervals, especially for the expected durations of the regimes.
  • Use Student-\(t\) state distributions with an AR(1) mean in each regime, or a Markov-switching GARCH model, to combine the interpretability of regimes with the responsiveness of GARCH.
  • Apply the same regime-switching approach to El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases in the Project 2 sea surface temperature data.

Link to the detailed analysis: Detailed analysis and code

Interactive app: JSE regime explorer (opens on shinyapps.io; it can take a few seconds to wake up). Code: scripts/shiny-app/ (see the code and data appendix).

Lecture 1

Date: 27 July 2026

Topic covered: Foundations

What I Did:

Plotted time series plots for discrete and continuous time series data: Section 1

What I Learned:

A time series is an ordered sequence of observations collected over time. The ordering matters since observations are often dependent on previous observations (sequential correlation).

Assumption

Equally spaced measurements.

Assumption

Autocorrelation across time.

A time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points through time to give a series of measurements through time.

Noise (stochastic) in data introduces different realisations. An observed time series is only one realisation of an underlying stochastic process. This is important as we are not just trying to model the observations but the process that generated them.

Questions:

Q: How does noise introduce different realisations?

A: In normal regression the pattern is fixed and the noise sits on top of it:

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i, \] where each error term is independent.

In an AR process the noise actually builds the pattern. This means that every apparent trend is made of past shocks that haven’t died away yet. A different set of shocks will give a different shape because the shape of the path comes from noise. It isn’t that time series errors are correlated but that each observation is a weighted sum of every past shock making observations correlated.

Lecture 2

Date: 3 August 2026

Topic covered: The Forecasting Problem

What I Did:

Looked at stationary AR processes: Section 1

What I Learned:

A forecast horizon is how far into the future you try to predict values. When looking at time series data we are looking for stable, informative patterns (not just a lot of data).

Forecasting vs Goal setting vs Planning

A forecast is a prediction about what will happen in the future based on evidence that we have (with some uncertainty). Goal setting is what we want to happen in the future and planning is how we reach our goal.

The uncertainty associated with forecasting gives rise to forecast intervals (not just point estimates).

A random walk is a process where memory is permanent. Every future shock accumulates endlessly resulting in forecast variance growing linearly. A stationary AR is a process where memory decays geometrically. Shocks die out, forcing the forecast back to the process mean.

Questions:

Q: If a process changes over time, at what point can we discard previous observations when forecasting?

A: This is decided by the model and is called the model’s memory. A mean benchmark will use every observation and just forecast the mean, the naive benchmark will use the most recent observation, exponential smoothing uses all observations but weights them differently (older observations are given less weight). You would also discard observations if a structural break occurs.

Note

When determining the number of observations to estimate the model (training set) more is usually better, unless the process has changed.

What to Do Next:

Exploring a Series

Lecture 3

Date: 17 August 2026

Topics covered: Exploring a Series, Benchmarks and Forecast Accuracy

What I Did:

Worked through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1

What I Learned:

Time domain looks at previous observations whereas the frequency domain looks at cycles at different frequencies. Often you will need to look at both of these domains.

Trend vs Seasonality vs Cycles

A trend is the long-run direction of movement in a time series. Seasonality models a pattern that repeats itself at a fixed AND known interval. A cycle is a long oscillation where the length is NOT fixed.

When dealing with time series data you may encounter changing variability. Here you need to transform the data to stabilise variance and difference to remove trend and seasonality. When structural breaks are present in the data you can either use an indicator variable at the break or you can fit separate models on either side of the break.

There are 4 benchmark forecasting models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift.

Residuals are not forecast errors

Residuals are for diagnostics; forecast errors are for evaluation!

You cannot run normal cross-validation on time series data since the ordering of observations matters. Future observations must never be used when estimating a forecasting model.

Questions:

Q: How do you identify a significant structural break?

A: This can be done using formal tests, dependent on whether the date of the break is known prior to looking at the data. If the date is known in advance (e.g. a policy change), you can use Chow’s test. Chow’s test fits the model before and after the date of the break and uses an F-test to check if there is a statistically significant difference in model parameters. If the date is unknown you can run a Chow test at every possible date and take the largest F, compared against adjusted critical values. This is a sup-F test and accounts for having searched over every date, making it harder to declare a break.

What to Do Next:

Operators, Stationarity and White Noise

Lecture 4

Date: 19 August 2026

Topic covered: Three Validation Strategies, Linear Models for the Conditional Mean

What I Did:

Continued working through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1

What I Learned:

Since you can’t perform regular cross-validation on time series data you use a different approach. Walk-forward validation advances the forecast origin one step at a time and re-estimates the model at each step. Expanding window validation keeps every historical observation while moving the forecast origin forward. Sliding window validation keeps the training window length fixed while moving the forecast origin forward.

Expanding window is good for stable processes whereas sliding window is good for rapidly changing processes.

We want our data to be stationary and for the residuals to be white noise. To restore stationarity you can transform the data to stabilise the variance and take linear/seasonal differences to remove trend and seasonality. Log-transformations reduce a multiplicative model to an additive model.

Weak white noise requires uncorrelated observations with zero mean and constant variance but strict white noise requires iid observations.

Questions:

Q: What is the difference between walk-forward and expanding window?

A: In the notes they are the same procedure: the training set always starts at \(y_1\) and grows by one observation each time the forecast origin moves forward. “Walk-forward” describes how the origin moves and “expanding window” describes what is kept. The slides list them as separate strategies, but note that they use the same growth rule. The difference is that walk-forward re-estimates the model at every step, so it has a higher computational cost. The real contrast is with the sliding window, which drops the oldest observation at each step.

Lecture 5

Date: 24 August 2026

Topic covered: Linear Models for the Conditional Mean

What I Did:

Fit both ARIMA and SARIMA to the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1

What I Learned:

The moving average, MA(\(q\)), model is driven by lagged shocks. The dependence is based on errors not actual observations. The model has short memory. An MA(\(q\)) is always stationary and is restricted to be invertible.

The autoregressive, AR(\(p\)), model regresses a series on its own path.

ARMA combines both MA and AR models and is fitted by maximum likelihood, not OLS, since the past shocks are never observed.

Note

ACF and PACF graphs are used to determine which ARMA model to fit. An AR(\(p\)) has a PACF that cuts off after lag \(p\). An MA(\(q\)) has an ACF that cuts off after lag \(q\).

The ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model allows for differencing and the SARIMA model includes seasonality.

Questions:

Q: How can you determine if there is additional seasonality in a dataset after differencing or if it is just noise? For example in Section 1, there were still spikes at some lags in the PACF after log-transforming and differencing the AirPassengers dataset.

A: You can check if the residuals look like white noise by using a Ljung-Box test. A non-significant test means that there is no evidence of remaining autocorrelation (even if there are still a few lags that spike in the ACF/PACF). At the 5% level about 1 in 20 lags will spike by chance.

Additional Lecture with Sulaiman

Date: 16 September 2026

Topic covered: Conditional Variance Models (ARCH and GARCH)

What I Did:

Worked through the provided Lab: Section 1

What I Learned:

All previous models have simply modelled the conditional mean and assumed constant variance. This fails for financial return data as it understates risk during periods where risk is highest and overstates risk when it is lowest. We now have both a mean (predictable component of the series) and a variance (conditional variance) equation.

Note

A series can be uncorrelated and still highly predictable in magnitude.

The ARCH model specifies conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations. The simplest case being \(\sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\).

Volatility clustering

Large changes tend to follow large changes and small changes tend to follow small changes. Returns are often uncorrelated, hence why the ACF of returns indicates very little, however squared returns can be strongly autocorrelated.

The GARCH model adds the previous conditional variance to the ARCH equation. This makes it equivalent to an ARCH model with infinite memory. A GARCH(1,1) model is usually sufficient in practice.

\[ \sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2, \] where \(\alpha_1\) measures how strongly volatility reacts to a new shock, \(\beta_1\) measures how long that reaction lasts, \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\) is the persistence.

Questions:

Q: Why must \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\)?

A: When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\) this ensures that the long-run variance is \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1- \alpha_1 - \beta_1}\) and that the process has a benchmark variance for the volatility to return to. When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 = 1\) (IGARCH) the shocks to volatility are permanent. This means that all the weight is on the past and none is on the long-run level. This is the variance equivalent of a random walk.

What to Do Next:

Spectral Analysis

Links: AI Log

Lecture 7

Date: 14 September 2026

Topic covered: Exponential Smoothing

What I Did:

Worked through Exponential Smoothing Exercises: Section 2

What I Learned:

Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations. Weights decrease exponentially the further back in time you go. The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) adjusts the weight put on past observations. A large \(\alpha\) puts a lot of weight on the most recent observation, similar to the Naive forecast. A small \(\alpha\) averages over a long history, similar to the Mean forecast. This is similar to GARCH but applied to observations instead of squared shocks.

SES vs Holt vs Holt-Winters

Simple exponential smoothing (SES) only updates a level resulting in flat forecasts. Holt’s method adds a trend equation, that describes the slope, so forecasts follow a straight line. Holt-Winters adds a seasonal equation. Each component gets its own smoothing parameter (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\)).

The smoothing parameters and initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\)) are estimated by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors. Fitted values are one-step-ahead forecasts, so residuals are always one-step-ahead errors.

To turn the exponential smoothing algorithm into a state-space model we can write it in error-correction form: \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\), \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\). This allows us to estimate \(\sigma\) and build prediction intervals.

This is what ets() does.

Prediction intervals are usually too narrow

Standard prediction intervals only capture the random error and ignore the uncertainty in parameter estimates and choice of model.

Questions:

Q: How do we get variances of SES forecasts (\(\sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]\)) if the point forecasts are flat?

A: The point forecast stays at \(\ell_T\), but every future error also moves the level by \(\alpha e_t\). These shifts add up, so uncertainty grows linearly with \(h\) even though the mean does not change.

What to Do Next:

Time Series Regression Models

Links: AI Log

Lecture 8

Date: 21 September 2026

Topic covered: Time Series Regression Models

What I Did:

Worked through Chapter 2: Time Series Regression Models and the provided slides, rerunning the R code that had been included. Used a Kalman filter to estimate regression coefficients in the US consumption example: Section 2

What I Learned:

Time Series Regression includes explanatory variables in time series models. This allows one to include trend and seasonality covariates in the model instead of just differencing the series to make it stationary.

ARMAX vs regression with ARMA errors

ARMAX includes lagged values of the response as predictors, \(y_t = \beta x_t + \phi y_{t-1} + \dots\). This means that \(\beta\) can no longer be interpreted as the effect of \(x\) on the mean of \(y\). Regression with ARMA errors keeps the normal regression equation and lets the errors follow an ARMA process, \(y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \eta_t\), where \(\eta_t\) follows an ARMA process. This means that \(\beta_1\) can still be interpreted in the usual way.

Harmonic regression assumes that the seasonal pattern stays the same over time.

Autocorrelated errors

When errors are autocorrelated, OLS still gives unbiased estimates but they are no longer efficient. The usual standard errors are also wrong, so tests and intervals are too optimistic.

Questions:

Q: When should I add a lagged response instead of modelling the errors as ARMA?

A: It depends on whether the dependence is part of the process or a nuisance. If \(y\) depends on its own past (e.g. a stock that accumulates), a lagged response makes sense, but then \(\beta_1\) is only the immediate effect of \(x\) and the long-run effect is \(\beta_1/(1-\phi)\). If the goal is the effect of \(x\) on the mean of \(y\), the errors should be modelled as ARMA. In Example 4.1 in Section 2, the data were generated with AR(1) errors, so the model with a lagged response was misspecified unless \(x_{t-1}\) was also included. Regression with AR(1) errors is the same as this model with the coefficient of \(x_{t-1}\) restricted to \(-\phi\beta_1\).

State-Space Models

Links: AI Log

Lecture 9

Date: 28 September 2026

Topic covered: State-Space Models

What I Did:

Worked through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2

What I Learned:

A state-space model has both an observation equation and a state equation.

The observation equation \(y_t = F\theta_t + v_t\) links what we observe to an unobserved state whereas the state equation \(\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t\) describes how the state changes over time.

Note

Regression, ARIMA and exponential smoothing models can all be written in state-space form. State-space models don’t need stationarity since trend and seasonality are modelled directly and allowed to change over time.

The Kalman filter is a recursive algorithm that first predicts and then updates. First the state, \(a_t, R_t\), and the next observation, \(f_t, Q_t\), are predicted. Then the state estimate, \(m_t, C_t\), is updated. The updated estimate is a weighted average of the prediction and the new observation where the Kalman gain decides how much weight is assigned to the observation.

Bayesian Framework

The Kalman filter works in a Bayesian way where, \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}\). The posterior becomes the prior of the next step.

Questions:

Q: How do I decide which variances in \(W\) should be allowed to be non-zero?

A: A non-zero variance lets that state change over time and a zero variance keeps it fixed. The structure of the model decides which states can have noise. In the CO\(_2\) model in Section 2 only the level, slope and current seasonal effect get noise, because the other seasonal states are just the previous effects shifted along. The size of the variances can then be estimated by maximum likelihood. If an estimated variance is essentially zero, that state can be fixed, and models can be compared with the likelihood or AIC, e.g. static (\(W = 0\)) vs time-varying coefficients in the US consumption example.

What to Do Next:

Kalman Filter

Links: AI Log

Lecture 10

Date: 5 October 2026

Topic covered: Kalman Filter

What I Did:

Continued working through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2

What I Learned:

The Kalman filter is used to filter and forecast in dynamic linear Gaussian systems. This filter is recursive so we can process new observations as they arrive. The Kalman smoother starts at the end of a series and works backwards. This is better for looking backwards (not prediction).

Filtering vs Smoothing vs Forecasting

If we estimate the state at time \(t\) using data up to time \(s\):

  • \(s < t\) = forecasting
  • \(s = t\) = filtering
  • \(s > t\) = smoothing

Forecasting and filtering are done using the Kalman filter. Smoothing is done using the Kalman smoother.

The likelihood is the product of one-step-ahead predictive densities, \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\). The unknown variances, \(V\) and \(W\), can be estimated by maximum likelihood.

Prediction intervals use \(Q_t = FR_tF' + V\). They are prediction intervals (not confidence intervals) because they are for a future observation and include the observation noise, \(V\), as well as the uncertainty about the state.

If there are missing observations present in the data, there is nothing to update with and the Kalman gain will be zero. Consecutive missing observations increase uncertainty.

Method
  1. The prior predicts the next state from the previous estimate of the state, with some uncertainty (state equation).
  2. The likelihood asks how likely the new observation is given all possible states (observation equation).
  3. The new posterior, for the current state, is given by combining the likelihood and the prior.

Questions:

Q: Why does the Kalman filter only work for linear Gaussian state-space models?

A: The Kalman filter does a linear transformation of a Gaussian which gives another Gaussian.

\[ \text{Gaussian prior} \times \text{Gaussian likelihood} \propto \text{Gaussian posterior} \] The Kalman filter only keeps track of the mean and variance. When we have a non-linear or non-Gaussian distribution we either end up with a skewed distribution or a posterior with no closed form.

What to Do Next:

Hidden Markov Models

Links: AI Log

Lecture 11

Date: 12 October 2026

Topic covered: Hidden Markov Models 1

What I Did:

Worked through Questions 1, 3, 4 and 7 of the HMM tutorial and wrote the forward algorithm from first principles: Section 2

What I Learned:

A hidden Markov model (HMM) has an unobserved state process, \(C_t\), that follows a Markov chain and an observed process, \(X_t\), whose distribution depends only on the current state. Each state has its own state-dependent distribution (e.g. Poisson or Gaussian).

Assumption

The next state only depends on the current state (Markov property).

The Markov chain is described by the transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\), where \(\gamma_{ij} = P(C_{t+1} = j \mid C_t = i)\), and the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\). A large diagonal in \(\Gamma\) means that the states are persistent.

Independent mixture vs HMM

An independent mixture draws a new state at every time point, independently of the last one. An HMM lets the state depend on the previous state, which creates autocorrelation in the observations.

The likelihood, \(L_T = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}'\), is calculated with the forward algorithm and maximised numerically. The forward probabilities are scaled at every step to avoid underflow.

Questions:

Q: Why does an HMM produce autocorrelated observations if the observations are conditionally independent given the states?

A: The observations are only independent once we know the states. A large observation makes a high-mean state more likely and, since the states are persistent, the next observation is likely to come from that same state.

What to Do Next:

Hidden Markov Models 2

Links: AI Log

Lecture 12

Date: 19 October 2026

Topic covered: Hidden Markov Models 2

What I Did:

Worked through Questions 2, 5 and 6 of the HMM tutorial, wrote the backward algorithm, local decoding and the Viterbi algorithm from first principles, and fitted Poisson HMMs to the earthquake counts: Section 2, Project 4

What I Learned:

Once an HMM has been fitted we usually want to know which state the process was in. This is called decoding.

Local vs global decoding

Local decoding finds the most likely state at each time point separately, using the forward and backward probabilities. Global decoding finds the most likely sequence of states using the Viterbi algorithm. The two can disagree.

The number of states is chosen with AIC or BIC. The likelihood of an HMM often has several local maxima, so the model should be fitted from several different starting values.

Questions:

Q: Why can’t short visits to a state be recovered by decoding?

A: A single visit to a state needs two unlikely transitions, there and back, and if the state-dependent distributions overlap, the observation is often also likely under the surrounding state. In the Viterbi exercise in Section 2, the single visit to state C at time 2 was decoded as A.

HMM toolkit

scripts/hmm-toolkit.R: my hidden Markov model functions (scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, the stationary distribution, the working-parameter transformation and matrix powers for forecasting). Used by Project 4 and the Hidden Markov Models part of Section 2.

hmm-toolkit.R 
# =============================================================================
# HMM toolkit, written from first principles (Time Series Analysis portfolio)
#
# Used by projects/project-04-analysis.qmd and section-2/section-2.qmd.
# Every function works with the matrix of state-dependent densities
# dens[t, i] = p_i(x_t), so the same code handles Poisson, Gaussian and
# categorical observations.
# =============================================================================

# Log-likelihood only (fast version, used inside optim()):
hmm_loglik = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  v = delta * dens[1, ]
  ll = log(sum(v))
  phi = v / sum(v)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      v = as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
      u = sum(v)
      ll = ll + log(u)
      phi = v / u
    }
  }
  ll
}

# Scaled forward algorithm: log-likelihood, log u_t, filtered probabilities and log alpha:
hmm_forward = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  phi_mat = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  lu = numeric(T_len)
  for (t in 1:T_len) {
    v = if (t == 1) delta * dens[1, ] else as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
    u = sum(v)
    lu[t] = log(u)                # log p(x_t | x_{1:t-1})
    phi = v / u                   # P(C_t = i | x_{1:t})
    phi_mat[t, ] = phi
  }
  list(loglik = sum(lu), lu = lu, phi = phi_mat,
       lalpha = cumsum(lu) + log(phi_mat))   # log alpha_t(i)
}

# Scaled backward algorithm: log beta (Zucchini et al., 2016):
hmm_backward = function(dens, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lbeta = matrix(0, T_len, m)     # log beta_T = 0
  phi = rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale = log(m)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      v = as.numeric(Gamma %*% (dens[t + 1, ] * phi))
      lbeta[t, ] = log(v) + lscale
      phi = v / sum(v)
      lscale = lscale + log(sum(v))
    }
  }
  lbeta
}

# Local decoding: P(C_t = i | x_{1:T}) = alpha_t(i) beta_t(i) / L_T:
hmm_local = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens, delta, Gamma)
  lbeta = hmm_backward(dens, Gamma)
  exp(fwd$lalpha + lbeta - fwd$loglik)
}

# Global decoding with the Viterbi algorithm (log scale):
hmm_viterbi = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lG = log(Gamma)
  ld = log(dens)
  xi = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  xi[1, ] = log(delta) + ld[1, ]
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      for (j in 1:m) {
        xi[t, j] = max(xi[t - 1, ] + lG[, j]) + ld[t, j]
      }
    }
  }
  # Back-tracing:
  states = numeric(T_len)
  states[T_len] = which.max(xi[T_len, ])
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      states[t] = which.max(xi[t, ] + lG[, states[t + 1]])
    }
  }
  list(states = states, xi = xi)
}

# Stationary distribution: solve delta (I - Gamma + U) = 1:
stat_dist = function(Gamma) {
  m = nrow(Gamma)
  solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
}

# Working (unconstrained) parameters -> transition probability matrix:
gamma_w2n = function(w, m) {
  G = diag(m)
  G[!G] = exp(w)                  # off-diagonal elements, relative to the diagonal
  G / rowSums(G)
}

# h-step transition matrix Gamma^h:
mat_pow = function(M, h) {
  R = diag(nrow(M))
  for (i in seq_len(h)) R = R %*% M
  R
}

precompute.R: fits the Gaussian HMMs (1 to 4 states) and GJR-GARCH, saves app_data.rds 
# =============================================================================
# JSE regime explorer: precompute the model fits used by app.R
#
# Run once from the root of the portfolio project (the folder with _quarto.yml):
#   source("scripts/shiny-app/precompute.R")
#
# It fits Gaussian HMMs with 1-4 states and GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t on the training
# set (Jul 1995 - Dec 2012), exactly as in the Project 4 analysis, runs every
# model through the whole series with the parameters fixed, and saves the
# results to scripts/shiny-app/app_data.rds. The app only reads that file, so
# it starts instantly and does not need rugarch or readxl when deployed.
# =============================================================================

library(readxl)
library(rugarch)

set.seed(2026)

data_path  = "_data/PT-DATA-ALBI-JIBAR-JSEIND-Daily-1994-2017.xlsx"
out_path   = "scripts/shiny-app/app_data.rds"
sheet_name = "JSE Various Indices"
train_end  = as.Date("2012-12-31")

if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("Could not find ", data_path, ". Run this script from the portfolio root folder.")
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# HMM toolkit (same functions as in project-04-analysis.qmd)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

hmm_loglik = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  v = delta * dens[1, ]
  ll = log(sum(v))
  phi = v / sum(v)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      v = as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
      u = sum(v)
      ll = ll + log(u)
      phi = v / u
    }
  }
  ll
}

hmm_forward = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  phi_mat = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  lu = numeric(T_len)
  for (t in 1:T_len) {
    v = if (t == 1) delta * dens[1, ] else as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
    u = sum(v)
    lu[t] = log(u)
    phi = v / u
    phi_mat[t, ] = phi
  }
  list(loglik = sum(lu), lu = lu, phi = phi_mat,
       lalpha = cumsum(lu) + log(phi_mat))
}

hmm_backward = function(dens, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lbeta = matrix(0, T_len, m)
  phi = rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale = log(m)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      v = as.numeric(Gamma %*% (dens[t + 1, ] * phi))
      lbeta[t, ] = log(v) + lscale
      phi = v / sum(v)
      lscale = lscale + log(sum(v))
    }
  }
  lbeta
}

hmm_local = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens, delta, Gamma)
  lbeta = hmm_backward(dens, Gamma)
  exp(fwd$lalpha + lbeta - fwd$loglik)
}

hmm_viterbi = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lG = log(Gamma)
  ld = log(dens)
  xi = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  xi[1, ] = log(delta) + ld[1, ]
  for (t in 2:T_len) {
    for (j in 1:m) xi[t, j] = max(xi[t - 1, ] + lG[, j]) + ld[t, j]
  }
  states = numeric(T_len)
  states[T_len] = which.max(xi[T_len, ])
  for (t in (T_len - 1):1) states[t] = which.max(xi[t, ] + lG[, states[t + 1]])
  states
}

stat_dist = function(Gamma) {
  m = nrow(Gamma)
  solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
}

gamma_w2n = function(w, m) {
  G = diag(m)
  G[!G] = exp(w)
  G / rowSums(G)
}

norm_hmm_nll = function(w, x, m) {
  mu = w[1:m]
  sigma = exp(w[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
  Gamma = if (m == 1) matrix(1) else gamma_w2n(w[(2 * m + 1):(2 * m + m * (m - 1))], m)
  delta = if (m == 1) 1 else stat_dist(Gamma)
  dens = sapply(1:m, function(j) dnorm(x, mu[j], sigma[j]))
  -hmm_loglik(matrix(dens, ncol = m), delta, Gamma)
}

norm_hmm_unpack = function(w, m) {
  mu = w[1:m]
  sigma = exp(w[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
  Gamma = if (m == 1) matrix(1) else gamma_w2n(w[(2 * m + 1):(2 * m + m * (m - 1))], m)
  ord = order(sigma)
  Gamma = Gamma[ord, ord, drop = FALSE]
  list(m = m, mu = mu[ord], sigma = sigma[ord], Gamma = Gamma,
       delta = if (m == 1) 1 else stat_dist(Gamma))
}

norm_dens = function(x, pars) {
  matrix(sapply(1:pars$m, function(j) dnorm(x, pars$mu[j], pars$sigma[j])), ncol = pars$m)
}

norm_pseudo = function(x, pars) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(norm_dens(x, pars), pars$delta, pars$Gamma)
  T_len = length(x)
  pred = rbind(pars$delta, fwd$phi[-T_len, , drop = FALSE] %*% pars$Gamma)
  cdf = matrix(sapply(1:pars$m, function(j) pnorm(x, pars$mu[j], pars$sigma[j])), ncol = pars$m)
  qnorm(pmin(pmax(rowSums(pred * cdf), 1e-10), 1 - 1e-10))
}

# Newey-West standard error of a mean (Bartlett kernel):
nw_se = function(d, L = 6) {
  n = length(d)
  u = d - mean(d)
  s = sum(u^2) / n
  for (l in 1:L) s = s + 2 * (1 - l / (L + 1)) * sum(u[-(1:l)] * u[1:(n - l)]) / n
  sqrt(s / n)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data (same cleaning as Projects 3 and 4)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

find_col = function(hdr, code, field) {
  idx = which(unlist(hdr[1, ]) == code & unlist(hdr[2, ]) == field)
  if (length(idx) != 1) stop(paste("Could not uniquely find", code, field))
  idx
}

hdr = read_excel(data_path, sheet = sheet_name, col_names = FALSE, n_max = 4)
raw = read_excel(data_path, sheet = sheet_name, col_names = FALSE, skip = 4,
                 na = c("#N/A", "", "NA"), guess_max = 10000)

date_col = which(sapply(raw, function(x) inherits(x, c("POSIXct", "Date"))))[1]
alsi_col = find_col(hdr, "J203:XJSE:IND", "TRI")

alsi = data.frame(date = as.Date(raw[[date_col]]), tri = as.numeric(raw[[alsi_col]]))
alsi = alsi[!is.na(alsi$date) & !is.na(alsi$tri), ]
alsi = alsi[order(alsi$date), ]
alsi = alsi[!duplicated(alsi$date), ]
alsi$r = c(NA, 100 * diff(log(alsi$tri)))
alsi = alsi[!is.na(alsi$r), ]

r_all   = alsi$r
n_train = sum(alsi$date <= train_end)
r_train = r_all[1:n_train]
train_idx = 1:n_train
test_idx  = (n_train + 1):length(r_all)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Gaussian HMMs with 1-4 states (same starting values as the analysis)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

jse_starts = list(
  c(mean(r_train), log(sd(r_train))),
  c(0.1, -0.1, log(0.8), log(2), rep(-3, 2)),
  c(0.1, 0.05, -0.3, log(0.6), log(1.1), log(2.5), rep(-4, 6)),
  c(0.12, 0.08, 0, -0.3, log(0.5), log(0.85), log(1.4), log(2.8), rep(-4, 12))
)

models = lapply(1:4, function(m) {
  message("Fitting the ", m, "-state HMM ...")
  fit = optim(jse_starts[[m]], norm_hmm_nll, x = r_train, m = m, method = "BFGS",
              control = list(maxit = 2000))
  pars = norm_hmm_unpack(fit$par, m)

  # Run through the whole series with the training parameters fixed:
  dens_all = norm_dens(r_all, pars)
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma)

  k = m^2 + m
  logL = -fit$value
  c(pars, list(
    logL        = logL,
    k           = k,
    AIC         = -2 * logL + 2 * k,
    BIC         = -2 * logL + k * log(n_train),
    convergence = fit$convergence,
    filtered    = fwd$phi,                                     # P(C_t | x_1:t)
    smoothed    = hmm_local(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma), # P(C_t | x_1:T)
    viterbi     = hmm_viterbi(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma),
    ls          = fwd$lu,                                      # one-step-ahead log scores
    pz          = norm_pseudo(r_train, pars)                   # pseudo-residuals (training)
  ))
})

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-t errors and an AR(1) mean (Project 3 model)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

message("Fitting GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t ...")
spec_gjr = ugarchspec(variance.model     = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
                      mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(1, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
                      distribution.model = "std")
gjr_fit = ugarchfit(spec = spec_gjr, data = r_train, solver = "hybrid")

spec_fixed = spec_gjr
setfixed(spec_fixed) = as.list(coef(gjr_fit))
gjr_filt = ugarchfilter(spec = spec_fixed, data = r_all)

gjr_mu    = as.numeric(fitted(gjr_filt))
gjr_sigma = as.numeric(sigma(gjr_filt))
gjr_ls    = log(ddist("std", y = r_all, mu = gjr_mu, sigma = gjr_sigma,
                      shape = coef(gjr_fit)["shape"]))

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Log-score comparison table
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

scores = do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(m) {
  d = models[[m]]$ls[test_idx] - gjr_ls[test_idx]
  data.frame(model = paste0("Gaussian HMM, ", m, " state", if (m > 1) "s" else ""),
             m = m,
             train = mean(models[[m]]$ls[train_idx]),
             test  = mean(models[[m]]$ls[test_idx]),
             diff  = mean(d),
             p     = 2 * pnorm(-abs(mean(d) / nw_se(d))))
}))
scores = rbind(scores, data.frame(model = "GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t", m = NA,
                                  train = mean(gjr_ls[train_idx]),
                                  test  = mean(gjr_ls[test_idx]),
                                  diff  = NA, p = NA))

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Save
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

app_data = list(
  series   = data.frame(date = alsi$date, r = r_all),
  n_train  = n_train,
  models   = models,
  gjr      = list(sigma = gjr_sigma, mu = gjr_mu, ls = gjr_ls, coef = coef(gjr_fit)),
  scores   = scores,
  created  = Sys.time(),
  versions = c(R = R.version.string, rugarch = as.character(packageVersion("rugarch")))
)

saveRDS(app_data, out_path)
message("Saved ", out_path, " (", round(file.size(out_path) / 1e6, 1), " MB).")

# Quick check against the Project 4 analysis (expected about -7276, -6660, -6551, -6514):
print(round(sapply(models, `[[`, "logL"), 1))
app.R: the Shiny app

# JSE regime explorer
# Hidden Markov models for daily FTSE/JSE All Share Index returns (Project 4)
#
# Run locally:  shiny::runApp("scripts/shiny-app")
# Data:         app_data.rds, created by precompute.R
# =============================================================================

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(bsicons)
library(plotly)

app_data = readRDS("app_data.rds")

series  = app_data$series
n_train = app_data$n_train
n_all   = nrow(series)
test_start = series$date[n_train + 1]
ann     = sqrt(252)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
